title: Digital Marketing Basics
summary: Learn to find the right customers, make a clear offer, create content with a phone, plan posts, advertise honestly and measure results with simple calculations.
audience: Small business owners, tutors, sellers, secondary and university students

lessons.title: Know your customer, make a clear offer

body.p: Marketing is helping the right people find out that you can solve a problem for them, and making it easy for them to say yes. It does not need a big budget. A tailor in Kumasi, a phone-repair stall in Nairobi, a home tutor in Lusaka and a girl selling braided hair services in Freetown all do marketing every time they tell a possible customer what they offer. This course teaches you to do it on purpose, honestly and with a phone.

body.h: Step 1: know who you are talking to

body.p: You cannot speak to everyone. Pick one main type of customer and learn about them. Ask: who are they, where are they (which town, which school or campus), what problem do they have, what do they already use, how much can they afford, and which apps do they check every day? You learn this by listening. Ask your last five customers why they chose you and what almost stopped them.

Example: Amina tutors Mathematics for WAEC candidates. She first said her customers were 'students'. After talking to ten parents she found the real buyers are parents of Senior Secondary 2 and 3 students who worry about failing Maths, can pay monthly, and read WhatsApp messages in the evening after work. Now she knows what to say, when to say it and what price to quote.

An offer is what you give, for what price, under what conditions. A weak offer is 'I do tailoring'. A strong offer is 'Ankara shirts sewn in 5 days, free fitting, pay half now and half on collection'. A good offer answers four questions in one breath: what is it, who is it for, why is it better or easier than the alternative, and what does it cost or how do they pay.

list: Benefit, not just feature: 'screen replaced while you wait, 3-month warranty' is better than 'we sell screens'.
Proof: a photo of your work, a real customer comment or the number of years you have done this.
Fair limits: say honestly what you cannot do, such as 'Delivery within Lagos Island only'.

body.p: A call to action (CTA) is the one next step you want the customer to take: 'Send the word ORDER to this WhatsApp number', 'Call before 6 pm to book', 'Visit us at Stall 14, Makola Market'. Give only one main CTA per post or message. Three different instructions confuse people and fewer take any action. Make the step small, specific and possible today.

steps: Write down your ideal customer in one sentence.
Write your offer in one sentence with what, who, price and one proof.
Add one CTA that starts with a verb (send, call, book, visit).
Read it aloud to a friend. If they cannot repeat it, shorten it.

body.tip: Test your message with the question 'So what?'. If a customer could reply 'so what?', add a benefit or a proof.

lessons.title: Content for social media and messaging apps

body.p: Content is anything you share to attract attention and build trust: photos, short videos, status updates, voice notes, price lists and customer stories. Good content does not only say 'buy now'. People follow businesses that teach, show real results and answer questions. A useful guide is to mix three types of content: helpful, trust-building and selling.

list: Helpful: tips that solve a small problem. A phone repairer shows how to protect a battery from heat. A tutor posts one past-paper question with the working steps.
Trust-building: your process, your workshop, before and after photos, a customer's thanks (with their permission), who you are.
Selling: a clear offer with price, how to order and a deadline if there truly is one.

body.p: A common rule of thumb is that most of your posts should help or build trust, and only some should sell. Treat this as a starting point, not a law. Watch which posts bring questions and orders, then do more of those.

Apps change their features and rules often, so do not build your business on one trick. Build on principles that work anywhere: use a clear first line, show the product or result quickly, keep the message short, use the language your customers use (English, Pidgin, Krio, Twi, Swahili, Spanish, Irish or Gaelic phrases where natural), and always tell people what to do next.

In chat-based selling, speed and tone matter. A customer who asks 'How much?' and gets a reply after two days has probably already bought elsewhere. Prepare saved replies for common questions such as prices, delivery, payment details and opening hours, but add the customer's name and answer their actual question. Never copy-paste so heavily that it feels like a machine.

Example: Kwame sells second-hand phones in Accra. A customer writes 'Good afternoon, do you have iPhone 11?'. A weak reply: 'Yes. 1200.' A better reply: 'Good afternoon Ama. Yes, I have two iPhone 11 units, 64 GB, both tested. Here are real photos. Price is GH₵1200 each with a 7-day return if it fails a test. Would you like to see it in person or have it delivered?'. The better reply answers, proves, states the price with conditions and gives one next step.

steps: Write a caption: first line grabs attention, middle gives one benefit, last line gives the CTA.
Check every fact: price, size, colour, stock, delivery time.
Reply to comments and messages within the time you promise.
Save your best questions from customers and turn each into a future post.

body.tip: Write as you speak to a customer in your shop. Plain, friendly and clear beats fancy words.

lessons.title: Photos and short video on a phone

body.p: A modern phone camera is enough to make your products look professional. What matters is light, background, focus and honesty. Customers cannot touch your product online, so your photo does the work of your shop window.

list: Light: use daylight near a window or doorway, not direct harsh sun and not a dark room. Face the light toward the product, not behind it.
Background: clear the clutter. A clean plain wall, a sheet or a board works. A tailor can hang the dress on a plain door rather than a busy room.
Steady and sharp: clean the lens with a soft cloth, hold the phone with both hands or lean on a table, and tap the screen to focus.
Angles: take the front, the back, a close-up of the detail and one showing size, for example next to a hand or a ruler.
Edit lightly: crop and slightly raise brightness. Do not change colours so much that the customer receives something different.

body.p: Short videos are very good for showing movement and trust: a phone being repaired, a dress being turned around, cooking a snack, a tutor explaining one idea in 40 seconds. Hold the phone sideways or upright depending on where you will post, record in good light, speak clearly and close to the phone, and start with the most interesting moment in the first few seconds. Keep it as short as the idea needs.

Phones with little storage or slow data are common. Free storage by moving old files to a computer or cloud, and use the phone's lower quality video setting if needed for sharing. Compress photos before sending over weak data, but keep originals for important work.

Photograph your real stock. If a photo is from the supplier or the internet, say so, otherwise customers may feel cheated. Do not use another person's photos or music without permission. Ask before filming or posting a customer's face, and never film children without a parent or guardian's clear permission. Remove anything private in the background, such as documents, number plates or other customers.

Example: Fatima sells hand-made soap in Kano. Her first photos were dark and cluttered. She moved to the doorway at 10 am, used a white cloth and took one front, one close-up of texture and one with a hand for size. She also wrote 'Photo shows actual soap, colour may vary slightly by batch'. Customers asked fewer questions about quality and she had fewer disputes.

steps: Clean the lens.
Find soft daylight and a plain background.
Take four angles and pick the best two.
Crop, lightly brighten, and check the colour looks true.
Add a short caption with price and CTA.

body.tip: Take a photo of every sale you deliver, with permission. It becomes proof for future customers.

lessons.title: A simple posting calendar and permission-based lists

body.p: Consistency beats bursts. A small business that posts three useful things every week is usually better off than one that posts twenty things on Monday and then disappears. A posting calendar is a simple plan that removes daily stress about what to share.

Choose how often you can realistically post. Three days a week is 3 x 4 = 12 posts in a four-week month. Give each day a job. For example: Monday helpful tip, Wednesday product or work in progress, Friday offer with a clear CTA. Write the topics in an exercise book, a phone notes app or a free spreadsheet. Prepare photos in one batch, for example on Sunday, so weekdays are easy.

list: Mark local moments: school resumption, exam seasons, Ramadan and Eid, Christmas, Easter, harvest times, back-to-campus, market days, public holidays in your country.
Leave one empty slot a week for news, questions or a customer story.
Review monthly: keep what worked, drop what did not.

body.p: A list of customers' phone numbers or email addresses is one of the most valuable things a small business owns, because you can reach people directly. But a list only works if people agreed to be on it. Ask clearly: 'May I send you offers and updates on WhatsApp? Reply YES. You can reply STOP at any time.' Keep a record of who agreed and when.

Do not add people to groups or broadcast lists without asking, do not buy lists of numbers, and do not collect addresses from customers' orders and then use them for something unrelated. Many countries, including those in the UK, Ireland and Spain, have data protection laws that require consent and a way to opt out, and countries such as Nigeria, Ghana and Kenya also have data protection laws. Rules differ, so learn the rules where you and your customers live. A safe habit everywhere is permission first, a clear opt-out, and respect when someone says stop.

Example: Tunde repairs laptops in Ibadan. After each repair he asks, 'Can I send you a maintenance reminder in six months?'. About one in three customers say yes, so his list grows with people who actually want his messages. When he sends a short reminder, many reply because they asked for it. Sending too often is also a problem, so limit messages to what you promised.

steps: Choose posting days you can keep for three months.
Assign a topic type to each day.
Batch your photos and captions once a week.
Ask for permission and record it.
Send list messages only for the reasons you promised, and honour STOP at once.

body.tip: Message every list member by name and only about things you said you would send. This keeps opt-outs low.

lessons.title: Honest advertising, consumer rules and reputation

body.p: Trust is your most valuable marketing asset, and dishonest marketing destroys it quickly. Honest advertising is not only the right thing to do. In most countries it is also a legal requirement. This lesson gives general principles. Laws differ between Nigeria, Ghana, Sierra Leone, Gambia, Kenya, Zambia, the UK, Canada, Spain and Ireland, so if you advertise regulated products such as food, medicine, finance, or you advertise to children, check the rules from your national consumer or advertising authority.

list: Be truthful: do not claim a product does something it does not. Do not promise cures, guaranteed results or guaranteed exam passes unless you can really guarantee them.
Show the full price: include delivery fees and conditions. Do not hide costs until the last step.
No fake pressure: 'Only 2 left' or 'Offer ends tonight' must be true.
No fake reviews: never write praise yourself or pay for false reviews. Do not delete honest complaints to hide them.
Be clear it is an ad: if you are paid or given free products to promote something, say so.
Respect others' work: do not copy another business's photos, name or logo.

body.p: Most customers check what other buyers say before they buy. Make it easy for happy customers to speak: after delivery, send a polite message such as 'Thank you for your order. If you are happy, would you share a short comment or photo? Only if you wish.' Ask for permission to repost their words.

When a negative review or complaint appears, reply publicly in a calm, short and helpful way, and move details to a private message. Do not argue or reveal the customer's personal information. Fix the problem if you can. Potential customers read your reply as much as the complaint.

Example: A customer in Lusaka posts that her dress arrived two days late. The seller replies: 'Sorry, Mulenga. The delivery was late and I should have warned you sooner. I have messaged you to arrange a discount on your next order. We now confirm delivery dates by message.' Readers see responsibility and improvement.

steps: Read your ad aloud and underline every claim.
For each claim ask: can I show proof today?
Add delivery cost, deadline and conditions.
Respond to feedback within one day, publicly short, privately in detail.

body.tip: A guarantee you cannot keep is worse than no guarantee. Promise less and deliver slightly more.

lessons.title: Measuring results: reach, clicks, conversion and cost

body.p: If you do not measure, you are guessing. You do not need advanced software. A notebook or a simple spreadsheet is enough. Always track four things: reach, clicks or enquiries, orders, and money spent.

list: Reach: how many people saw your post or message.
Clicks or enquiries: how many took the first step, such as tapping a link or sending a message.
Click rate = clicks divided by reach, times 100.
Conversion rate = buyers divided by clicks or enquiries, times 100.
Cost per customer = total money spent divided by number of new customers.

body.p: Example 1. A post reached 2,000 people and 150 tapped to message you. Click rate = 150 / 2,000 = 0.075 = 7.5%.
Example 2. Of those 150 enquiries, 6 people bought. Conversion rate = 6 / 150 = 0.04 = 4%.

Example 3. You spent 3,000 on an advert and won 5 new customers. Cost per customer = 3,000 / 5 = 600. Now compare to profit. If you earn 1,200 profit from a sale and 600 went on advertising, you keep 600. If cost per customer were 1,500, you would lose money on the first sale, which only makes sense if customers usually come back.
Example 4. You send a message to a permission list of 500 people and 30 reply. Reply rate = 30 / 500 = 6%.

Numbers tell you where the problem is. High reach but few clicks means your picture or first line is weak. Many clicks but few buyers means the offer, price or reply speed needs work. Cost per customer too high means target the audience better or lower the spend. Change one thing at a time so you know what caused the change, and give each test enough time and enough people before deciding. Very small numbers can mislead: 1 sale out of 3 enquiries is not proof of 33% forever.

Compare two options fairly. Advert A cost 2,400 and brought 6 customers: 400 each. Advert B cost 3,000 and brought 10 customers: 300 each. B costs more in total but less per customer, so B is better value, assuming the customers are of similar quality.

steps: Write your four numbers for each campaign.
Calculate the three rates and cost per customer.
Compare with last month.
Decide one change to test next.

body.tip: Ask every new customer 'How did you find us?' and record the answer. It costs nothing and shows where customers come from.

quiz.q: Amina tutors Maths. Talking to ten families, she learns the people who pay are parents of exam-year students, not the students. What should she do?
options: Stop talking to customers and copy a bigger tutor's posts
Keep writing for students only because they use the service
Write her offers for parents, with prices and times that suit them
Lower her price without changing the message

quiz.q: Which of these is the strongest call to action for a tailor's post?
options: Please support us and share, follow, comment and visit
Message ORDER on WhatsApp before Friday to book your fitting
We are the best tailors in town
Contact us sometime if you like

quiz.q: A post reached 2,000 people and 150 sent a message. What is the click or enquiry rate?
Of 150 enquiries, 6 people bought. What is the conversion rate and what does it suggest?
options: 25%; the offer is clearly perfect
4%; it could mean the offer, price or reply speed needs checking
6%; always increase reach first
4%; it proves advertising does not work

quiz.q: You spent 3,000 on an advert and gained 5 new customers. Each sale earns 1,200 profit before advertising. What is cost per customer, and profit per first sale after advertising?
options: 600 and 0

quiz.q: Advert A cost 2,400 and brought 6 customers. Advert B cost 3,000 and brought 10 customers. Which is better value?
options: B, because it costs 300 per customer against 400 for A
A, because 6 is a smaller number
Neither, because their totals differ
A, because its total cost is lower

quiz.q: A phone-repair stall wants to start a customer broadcast list. Which approach is best?
options: Buy a list of numbers from a stranger in the market
Add every number from the repair book to a group
Ask after each repair whether they agree to receive updates, record the yes, and honour STOP
Add customers first and let them leave if they dislike it

quiz.q: Your post says 'Only 2 left, offer ends tonight' but you have 40 in stock and will repeat the offer next week. What is wrong?
options: It is fine if the price is low
Nothing, urgency always helps sales
It is false pressure; urgency claims must be true
It is only a problem on television

quiz.q: A customer posts a fair complaint that her order was late. What is the best public reply?
options: Tell her she is lying and list her details
Post a fake five-star review to cover it
Delete the post so no one sees it
A short apology, an explanation, and a private message to fix it

quiz.q: Fatima's soap photos look dark and cluttered. Which change helps most?
options: Photograph near a window or doorway with a plain background and focus on the soap
Add a bright filter that changes the colour
Use a supplier photo and say nothing
Take photos at night with a torch directly on the soap

quiz.q: Before filming a customer wearing the dress you made and posting it, what should you do?
options: Post it and remove it if they complain
Post it, because the dress is yours
Crop the face and hope no one notices
Ask for permission, and get a parent or guardian's permission if the person is a child

quiz.q: You can post 3 days a week for 4 weeks. How many posts do you need to plan, and what is the best way to prepare?
options: 12 posts, written fresh each morning in a rush
3 posts, repeated daily
12 posts, with photos and captions batched once a week
20 posts, all published on the first day

quiz.q: You sent a message to a permission list of 500 people and 30 replied. A friend says 6% is too low, so he suggests sending messages daily. What is the best judgement?
options: 30/500 is 6%, which may be fine for a list; sending too often can cause opt-outs, so test one change at a time
Daily messages always raise replies
Buy more numbers to replace the ones that did not reply
6% proves the list is useless

quiz.q: Many people tap your link but few buy. Which is the most sensible first step?
options: Spend double on reach
Check the offer, price, page clarity and how fast you reply to enquiries
Change the logo, photos, price and caption all at once
Delete all your posts

quiz.q: Which statement about rules on advertising is the most sensible?
options: Rules never apply to small online sellers
Only large companies can be punished
All countries have exactly the same rules, so learn one
General honesty principles apply widely, but you should check the rules in your country, especially for food, medicine, finance or ads to children
